title: Hinduism: you are that
hook: a father dissolves salt in water to show his son the hidden essence: that is you (Chandogya Upanishad 6.13)
tomorrow: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharma, what holds the world up. Your line was my own dharma. Day two hundred thirty-four.

A young man comes home after twelve years away at school. He's twenty-four, he's learned all the texts, and, the story says, he's a bit full of himself. His father, a teacher named Uddalaka, asks him one question: did you learn the thing by which everything else becomes known? The son, Shvetaketu, has no idea what he means. So his father starts teaching him again, from scratch, with ordinary things from the kitchen. A seed. Some honey. A river. And a lump of salt.
screen: `HOME FROM SCHOOL, A BIT PROUD.` → `THE THING THAT MAKES ALL KNOWN.` → `A LUMP OF SALT.`

segments.voice: This is from the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the Hindu scriptures that explore the self and ultimate reality. Uddalaka tells his son: put this salt in a cup of water tonight, and bring it to me in the morning. In the morning he says, bring me the salt. The son looks. It's gone. Taste the water from the top, says his father. Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, though you can't see it anywhere. That, says Uddalaka, is how it is with the finest essence of all things, what later Hindu teachers call Brahman, ultimate reality. Unseen, yet here, in everything. That is the real. That is the self. And then: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. The father says it again and again through this chapter, once after each picture. Hindu schools read these three words differently. Advaita Vedanta, following the teacher Shankara, reads them as identity: your deepest self and Brahman are one and the same. The school of Ramanuja reads a close unity with a difference, the self belonging to Brahman the way a body belongs to its soul. The school of Madhva holds that the self and God are always distinct, and reads the line another way. All three are Hindu, and all three take the salt seriously: something invisible, in every drop.
screen: `A LUMP OF SALT, OVERNIGHT.` · `TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM: SALTY.` · `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.` · `SHANKARA, RAMANUJA, MADHVA.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: If you have a glass of water and a pinch of salt, stir it in and take a slow sip; if not, just imagine it. You can't see the salt, yet every sip carries it. Close your eyes and let the father's picture sit with you; you don't need to decide what it means.
Brahman. Ultimate reality, invisible yet present in everything, the way salt is in every drop of the water it's dissolved in. Today's word.
Your line: you are that. Gone from sight, and in every drop. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the great sayings of the Upanishads; Hindu students of Vedanta study it with a teacher, and the schools of Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each explain it in their own way.

fork.setup: you're Shvetaketu. your father asks you to bring back the salt you put in water last night. what happens?
options: you can't find it, but every sip is salty.
fork.reveal: the salt is gone from sight but present everywhere. that, says Uddalaka, is how the finest essence is in all things: tat tvam asi.
